content: Hepatitis A is a viral infection that can lead to liver disease. The hepatitis A virus is present in the stool and blood of individuals who are infected. It is transmissible from one person to another. You can contract hepatitis A if you: Consume food or beverages contaminated with the virus. Touch objects contaminated with the virus and then place your hands in your mouth. Have close personal contact with an infected individual, such as providing care for them. Engage in sexual activity with an infected person. Symptoms of hepatitis A can develop rapidly and may include fever, fatigue, loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, dark urine, diarrhea, pale or clay-colored stools, joint pain, and jaundice (yellowing of the skin and eyes). Most older children and adults who contract hepatitis A experience illness for several weeks but typically recover without long-term liver damage. However, children under the age of six often do not exhibit symptoms. In rare cases, hepatitis A can result in liver failure and death, particularly in older adults and individuals with pre-existing liver conditions. Hepatitis A is prevalent in many countries worldwide. Anyone who has not been vaccinated or previously infected is at risk of contracting the virus. Travelers are at an increased risk, especially if they visit rural or remote areas, travel in regions with poor sanitation, or consume food and drinks in such settings. However, even travelers staying in urban areas, resorts, or luxury accommodations who practice good hygiene and are cautious about food and drink choices have been known to contract the virus in countries where hepatitis A is common. The most effective way to prevent hepatitis A is through vaccination. The hepatitis A vaccine is highly effective and has been part of routine childhood immunization schedules since 1996. It is recommended for international travelers aged six months or older who are visiting countries where hepatitis A is common. The vaccine is administered in two doses. If you are unable to complete both doses before traveling, receiving at least one dose as soon as possible before your trip can still provide protection. Infants aged 6 to 11 months should receive the vaccine if traveling to areas where hepatitis A is a concern, but this dose does not count toward the routine two-dose series. For individuals allergic to vaccine components or those younger than six months, a single dose of immune globulin can be administered. This provides effective protection for up to two months, depending on the dosage. Consult your healthcare provider to determine if this is the best option for you. Additional protection against hepatitis B can be achieved with a combination vaccine for hepatitis A and B, typically given in three doses. If your travel plans are imminent, discuss accelerated dosing of the combination vaccine with your doctor.
